problem: MLLM embodied agents facing ambiguous instructions (e.g. 'find the cup' with several cups) either hallucinate a target or brute-force physical search, and prior interactive agents treat dialogue as an isolated module with no unified model of navigation, human-attention and memory costs.
motivation: In the physical world, movement is expensive, asking a human has a social cost, and recalling memory is nearly free, yet next-token-trained MLLMs are 'cost-blind'. The paper argues that disambiguation is a cost-aware reasoning problem: the agent should weigh information gain against heterogeneous costs before moving.
key_idea: Unify Ask, GetMemory, Navigate and Found in one MLLM action space and train it with a critic-free GRPO variant (HC-GRPO) whose trajectory reward is task success minus heterogeneous action costs.
insight: The gain comes mainly from the RL stage's cost-aware shift toward cheap actions: relative to SFT-only, HC-GRPO raises SR from 59.2 to 61.5 and cuts TTC from 2.3 to 1.6, shifting actions from Navigate to GetMemory. Ablations show dialogue is indispensable (SR 10.5% without Ask) and memory saves cost (SR 52.0%, TTC 2.3 without it). Caveats: gains in SR over the best baselines are small, and the main advantage is in cost. Some numbers in the text (SFT TTC 2.4→1.8 in the synthesis paragraph vs 2.3→1.6 in the ablation) are inconsistent.
method: Unified reasoning core: Qwen2.5-VL-7B outputs a CoT trace and one action per step from multimodal context, with Navigate(loc), Ask(query), GetMemory(key), Found(target)
Heterogeneous cost function: Navigate cost = c_nav*distance, Ask cost = c_ask*(1+α*N_ask) with fatigue, memory = c_mem, with c_nav > c_ask >> c_mem; trajectory reward R = R_task − λ ΣC
HC-GRPO: samples G trajectories per instruction, uses group-normalized advantage (no value critic), PPO-style clipping and KL to the SFT reference policy
Two-stage training: SFT-CoT warm start on 800 oracle-planner trajectories with LLM-written rationales, then online HC-GRPO in the simulator
Episodic memory loop: observations from exploration are written to memory and retrievable via GetMemory

ESearch-Bench: AI2-THOR, ambiguity sets of 2-5 same-category candidates, Gemini-1.5-Pro-synthesized instructions, a simulated oracle user with decaying helpfulness (fatigue), and A* Navigate primitives

setting.training_data: 800 oracle SFT trajectories with CoT (LLM-annotated), then online RL in 80 AI2-THOR training scenes
setting.observation: egocentric RGB view plus the ambiguous instruction, dialogue history and episodic memory; scene graph and target ID hidden
setting.action_space: high-level semantic primitives: Navigate(loc) via A*, Ask(query), GetMemory(key), Found(target)
setting.privileged: none at test time (oracle planner used only to generate SFT data; simulated user oracle answers questions)

numbers.eval_set_note: 330 tasks in 30 unseen AI2-THOR scenes; mean over five seeds
numbers.extra: 800 SFT trajectories + online RL; simulated oracle user with fatigue
numbers.evidence: Table 1 main results under different numbers of distractors; ESearch-R1 row

numbers_note: Bench is the authors' own ESearch-Bench (not a standard benchmark). The cost sensitivity study and the action distribution are given only as figures. The text has inconsistent SFT TTC values (2.3 in the ablation vs 2.4→1.8 in the synthesis paragraph).
results: On ESearch-Bench, ESearch-R1 reaches 61.5% SR and 1.6 TTC (SwC 0.59) vs the strongest baseline ReAct Qwen2.5-VL-32B at 60.0% SR / 3.3 TTC / 0.36 SwC, roughly halving cost. It also beats Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash ReAct (SwC 0.45/0.46), Embodied-Reasoner (0.32) and Ask-To-Act (0.28). The shortest average trajectory is 4.3 steps.
limitations: Evaluated only in a single self-built AI2-THOR benchmark with abstracted navigation primitives and a simulated oracle user; no real robot or real human.
Static cost coefficients, perception errors, and 7B inference latency; SR gains over the best baselines are marginal and some reported numbers are inconsistent.
Baselines are adapted to the authors' action space and data, so the comparison is partly self-defined; the benchmark is small (330 tasks).
